title: Rāya Asoko: the only portrait that names Ashoka
seo_title: Rāya Asoko: the only inscribed portrait of Emperor Ashoka (Kanaganahalli)
meta_description: At Kanaganahalli in Karnataka, a carved panel labelled 'Rāya Asoko' in Brāhmī is the only known portrait that names Ashoka. Who made it, when, and why it matters.
og_title: The only portrait that names Ashoka
og_description: Two words in Brāhmī, 'Rāya Asoko', on a stupa panel in Karnataka. It was carved centuries after Ashoka died. Here is the evidence.
summary: Ashoka left dozens of inscriptions across the subcontinent, yet almost none of them uses his name, and no likeness of him made in his lifetime is known. The one carved portrait that names him, with the Brāhmī label rāya asoko, 'King Ashoka', was found on a ruined stupa at Kanaganahalli, near Sannati in Karnataka, during excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India that began in 1994. It shows how Buddhists of the Sātavāhana age remembered him, some three to four centuries after his death.

sections.h2: A king who rarely used his name
paras: Ashoka, the third Maurya emperor, ruled from about 268 to 232 BCE. His edicts on rocks and pillars run from Afghanistan to Karnataka, but in almost all of them he calls himself devānaṃpiya piyadasi: 'Beloved of the Gods', Piyadasi. Soon after James Prinsep deciphered Brāhmī in 1837, scholars linked this Piyadasi with Ashoka through the Sri Lankan chronicles. The stones themselves, though, kept the name back.

That changed in January 1915, when a mining engineer named Beadon found a minor rock edict at Maski, in today's Raichur district of Karnataka. It begins devānaṃpiyasa asokasa, 'of the Beloved of the Gods, Asoka'. Only a handful of Ashoka's own inscriptions use the name at all: versions of his minor rock edicts at Maski, Gujarra (Madhya Pradesh), Nittur and Udegolam (Karnataka).

His face is missing too. Mauryan coins are punch-marked with symbols, not royal portraits, and no statue or painting made in his lifetime survives. So whatever we picture when we say 'Ashoka' comes from later hands.

The trail to the portrait begins in a temple. In 1986 the roof of the Kali shrine in the Chandralamba temple complex at Sannati, on the Bhima river in Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, collapsed and damaged the image. When the image was moved, the stone slab on which it had stood turned out to carry Ashokan edicts in Brāhmī script and Prakrit language. The slab had served as a pedestal, unread, for a very long time.
That find turned attention to the surroundings. About three kilometres away, near the village of Kanaganahalli, lay a low mound beside the river.

sections.h2: The great stupa by the Bhima
paras: The Archaeological Survey of India began excavating the Kanaganahalli mound in 1994, under K. P. Poonacha, and the work continued in seasons into the early 2000s. The mound was a Buddhist stupa, cased in carved limestone slabs. The excavation report, Excavations at Kanaganahalli, was published as Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India no. 106 (imprint 2011).

The site yielded well over a hundred short inscriptions in Brāhmī script and Prakrit language, from about the 1st century BCE onwards, many of them naming donors. Kings appear on the slabs with labels; one names Simuka, remembered as the founder of the Sātavāhana dynasty. Monika Zin's 2018 study of the 60 large slabs that once covered the dome reconstructs their original sequence and reads each scene against Buddhist texts.
Kanaganahalli belongs to the Andhra tradition of stupa building, alongside Amaravati, yet scholars stress how unusual it is.

sections.h2: The panel: a king, a queen and a parasol
paras: Among the slabs is a damaged panel showing a royal couple at the centre. The king wears a turban and large earrings, and a parasol, the old sign of sovereignty, is held over him. His queen is beside him, and attendants hold the parasol and a fly-whisk (chāmara). Along the border above, a single line in Brāhmī reads rāya asoko: 'King Ashoka'.

Panels at Sanchi and Amaravati are often identified as Ashoka, and with good reason, but none of them carries his name. At Kanaganahalli the sculptor removed the doubt. It is, so far, the only known portrait of the emperor with an inscription naming him.

sections.h2: A portrait made by people who never saw him
paras: The panel is not a likeness. The historian Nayanjot Lahiri dates it to the 2nd century CE, and scholars generally place the Kanaganahalli reliefs in the early centuries CE: some three to four centuries after Ashoka's death. The people who carved it had never seen him. What they had was memory: Buddhist traditions, later gathered in texts such as the Aśokāvadāna, remembered Ashoka as the model Buddhist king, and Sātavāhana-period donors set him among the kings shown on their great stupa.

That is what makes the panel valuable. It does not tell us what Ashoka looked like. It tells us how he was remembered, and that this memory was alive in northern Karnataka, the same region where his own edicts at Maski, Sannati and elsewhere had been cut into stone centuries earlier.

sections.h2: How to read two words of Brāhmī
paras: Brāhmī is read from left to right. Each consonant sign carries a built-in short 'a'. To give it another vowel, the scribe adds a small stroke to the consonant; a vowel at the start of a word has a letter of its own. So rāya asoko is written with five signs: rā (r with the long-ā stroke), ya (plain y, its 'a' understood), a (the letter for initial a), so (s with the o-stroke) and ko (k with the o-stroke).

Notice the language, too. Rāya is a Prakrit word for 'king', related to Sanskrit rājan; asoko is the Prakrit form of Aśoka. Books do not always agree on how to print the label (some textbooks and exam guides print rānyo), which is exactly why epigraphists go back to the stone, or to a good photograph of it, before they quote a single letter.

Kanaganahalli is a protected site of the Archaeological Survey of India in Chitapur taluk, Kalaburagi district, near Sannati. The Hindu reported in 2024 on years of neglect at the site and on new conservation work. Check access with the ASI's Hampi Circle before you travel.

If two words of Brāhmī can rewrite how we picture an emperor, the rest of the script is worth an evening. Talaash Heritage's [Introduction to Brāhmī script](write-like-asoka-s-scribes-a-brahmi-workshop.html) teaches you to read Ashoka's own letters, and our guides to [Ashoka and his edicts](ashoka-and-his-edicts.html) and the [Brāhmī script](brahmi-script.html) go further. Talaash Lectures #3, 'Read Brāhmī, a first lesson', follows on Sunday 6 December.

faq.q: Is there any portrait of Ashoka made in his lifetime?
faq.a: None is known. Mauryan coins carry punch-marked symbols rather than royal faces, and no statue or painting of Ashoka from his own time survives. The Kanaganahalli panel was carved some three to four centuries later.
'King Ashoka'. Rāya is a Prakrit word for king (Sanskrit rājan) and asoko is the Prakrit form of Aśoka. It is written in Brāhmī script.
On the Bhima river near Sannati, in Chitapur taluk of Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, northern Karnataka. It is an Archaeological Survey of India site.

faq.q: Which of Ashoka's own inscriptions use his name?
faq.a: Only a few: versions of his minor rock edicts at Maski (found in 1915), Gujarra, Nittur and Udegolam. Elsewhere he calls himself devānaṃpiya piyadasi, 'Beloved of the Gods'.
